title: Thailand Looks to Russia for Energy as Hormuz Ceasefire Expires; Gulf Producers Drill Through the War
subhead: Bangkok signals a pivot toward Russian gas, oil and fertilizer after the Middle East crisis exposed its 50% dependence on Gulf supplies, even as the US-Iran ceasefire lapses and oil climbs above $91. Meanwhile ADNOC and Gulf producers keep expanding output through the conflict.

sections.heading: Thailand Pivots Toward Russian Energy After Hormuz Disruption
sections.body: Thailand's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told TASS that the Middle East crisis has forced Bangkok to diversify its energy imports, explicitly naming Russia as a target for gas, oil and fertilizer. Thailand currently meets about 50% of its energy needs through Middle Eastern countries, and the recent difficulties with tankers transiting the blocked Strait of Hormuz exposed that concentration risk. Phuangketkeow said the two sides have already discussed financial mechanisms for trade under current restrictions, acknowledging obstacles but insisting Moscow and Bangkok can still use acceptable and permitted payment channels.
sections.whyItMatters: A major Asian importer is openly courting Russian energy as a hedge against Gulf instability — a concrete sign that the Hormuz crisis is redrawing Asian supply relationships in Moscow's favor, not just rerouting Western flows.

sections.heading: US-Iran Ceasefire Expires, Oil Climbs Above $91
sections.body: The fragile 60-day US-Iran ceasefire expired Monday with no deal, and oil prices responded. Brent crude rose 0.2% to $91.06 a barrel in Asian trading Tuesday after gaining more than $2 on Monday, with WTI reaching its highest level since late July, according to Reuters and Firstpost. Iran said it would shift to a 'fully offensive' military posture if diplomacy fails, while President Trump ruled out extending the interim deal and demanded Iran's surrender. Shipping through Hormuz has collapsed: Reuters reported only five tankers passed the strait on Saturday and none on Sunday, versus 31 the previous weekend. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd continue using alternative land routes.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is now pricing renewed supply risk without a diplomatic backstop. The near-total halt in Hormuz tanker traffic — even as the war pauses — shows how fragile the corridor remains and how quickly a full blockade could return.

sections.heading: Gulf Producers Drill Through the War: ADNOC Expands Output
sections.body: While the conflict rages, Gulf producers are expanding. Reuters reports ADNOC has boosted oil output despite the Iran war, emerging as one of the Gulf's most flexible exporters thanks to geography, defense capabilities and a willingness to take risks. A Reuters analysis described the Emirates giant as 'unbound' after its OPEC exit, launching on a quest for growth. The broader trend is confirmed by market commentary noting Gulf states are ramping up spending on oil and gas projects through the conflict, with analysts flagging stocks that benefit from the drilling push.
sections.whyItMatters: The war is not deterring Gulf investment — it is accelerating it. Producers outside the immediate conflict zone are positioning to capture market share and premium pricing that the disruption creates, a quiet reshaping of the region's export hierarchy.

sections.heading: Russia's Fuel Shortage Deepens: Indian Gasoline Stuck in Murmansk
sections.body: Russia's refining crisis is worsening. Ukraine's summer campaign against Russian refineries has pushed fuel shortages into at least 10 regions, now reaching the Moscow region, with gasoline sales on the St. Petersburg exchange down an average 20% since the start of August, per Oilprice.com citing Reuters. Russia received its first gasoline cargo from India — a roughly 68,000-metric-ton shipment produced by Nayara Energy at its Vadinar refinery, delivered to the Arctic port of Vitino after a ship-to-ship transfer at Port Said. But NV.ua reports the Indian gasoline destined for Russia is stuck in Murmansk as the shortage remains unresolved. The latest major casualty is the 120,000-barrel-per-day Orsk refinery, which could stay offline up to six months after an August 11 attack. Russian seaborne petroleum-product exports fell 33.3% in July from June and 54.7% year-on-year, per Reuters calculations based on LSEG data.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is now importing fuel by sea from Asia to plug domestic gaps — a striking reversal for a major exporter. The Murmansk bottleneck shows the logistical strain, and the reliance on Indian refineries that themselves run on Russian crude highlights the circular, sanctions-adjacent nature of the trade.

sections.heading: Washington Weighs Sanctions That Could Catch China in the Crossfire
sections.body: As the ceasefire lapses, the US is preparing a new wave of economic pressure on Iran that could reach beyond Tehran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration is preparing measures 'never seen' that could be announced as soon as next week, per Reuters. The most consequential target could be China's independent 'teapot' refineries, which purchase more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil and are crucial to Tehran's crude revenue. IBTimes reports Washington could expand secondary sanctions against buyers of Iranian oil, and Treasury has already warned two larger Chinese banks they could face secondary sanctions if Iranian funds move through their systems. OFAC has sanctioned more than 1,000 people, vessels and aircraft since Trump's second term began, and US measures have frozen an estimated $500 billion in Iran-linked cryptocurrency.
sections.whyItMatters: The next escalation is aimed as much at China as at Iran. Targeting teapot refiners and Chinese banks would test how far Washington is willing to go to choke Iranian revenue — and whether Beijing absorbs the cost or pushes back on the energy trade.

sections.heading: The Americas' Challenge to Middle East Oil Supremacy
sections.body: Bloomberg Opinion notes that for a few weeks of 2026, the American continents were pumping nearly half of the world's oil — an extraordinary moment that reflects how the Iran war and Hormuz disruption are accelerating the shift of supply away from the Gulf. The US Energy Secretary touted record oil production in a Midland, Texas address, downplaying price concerns even as high gas prices persist amid the war. This Americas supply surge is a structural counterweight to Gulf disruption, giving importers alternatives as Hormuz traffic stalls.
sections.whyItMatters: The war is accelerating a supply rebalancing that favors the Western Hemisphere. As Gulf exports face disruption, US and Latin American barrels are filling the gap — a shift that outlasts any ceasefire and reshapes who sets the marginal price of oil.

bottomLine: The US-Iran ceasefire expired with no deal, sending Brent above $91 and nearly halting Hormuz tanker traffic — but the more consequential moves are happening at the margins. Thailand is openly courting Russian energy to hedge its 50% Gulf dependence, Gulf producers like ADNOC are expanding output through the war, and Washington is preparing sanctions that could hit Chinese teapot refiners. Russia, meanwhile, is importing Indian gasoline by sea as Ukrainian strikes cripple its refineries. The conflict is no longer just a supply shock — it is actively redrawing Asian supply relationships, Gulf export hierarchies and the US-China energy trade.
sources: TASS, Reuters, Oilprice.com, Firstpost, IBTimes, NV.ua, Bloomberg Opinion, Kyiv Post, MSN/Morningstar, Fox News, The Hindu
